title: Exclusivity/ownership markers must be validated by structurally observable proof
requirement: Where a Clank uses an exclusivity or ownership marker (a run lock, lease, or ownership record) to coordinate execution across process or execution-context boundaries, that marker's validity MUST be determinable from state the granting authority itself observes, not inferred by the validating context from a reusable or context-ambiguous identifier. Reclaiming a marker (treating its prior owner as no longer holding it) MUST rest on grantor-observable proof of the owner's death or expiry. Honoring a marker as currently held, and any action taken on the strength of that marker (including terminating or otherwise acting on the process it identifies), MUST rest on that same standard of proof. Marker validity is a property of the granting mechanism (a kernel handle dies with the process that holds it; a database session lock dies with the connection; a lease expires against a clock the grantor controls) — never an inference the validating context draws on its own from an identifier the mechanism did not itself vouch for.
trigger: Applies to any Clank that uses an exclusivity/ownership marker capable of outliving, or being interpreted across, more than one process or execution context — a run lock, lease, or ownership record consulted by code other than the process that created it, or consulted after that process may have exited. Purely in-process locking, where the marker cannot outlive the context that validated it, is out of scope by trigger. A Clank with no exclusivity/ownership marker at all is out of scope.
rationale: Four independent-environment discoveries of the identical unsoundness: a crashed run left a lock recording PID 1, and every subsequent hourly scheduler fire for roughly 81 consecutive attempts concluded the prior run was still alive and refused to start, because every container is PID 1 to itself; the inverse failure, where a liveness check keyed on a recorded PID could terminate an unrelated process that had since reused that PID; the same PID/hostname-based reclaim logic independently proven unsound in a one-shot container runtime; and a stale PID file that let a health-check process spawn a duplicate daemon against the same production database because the file's PID no longer identified anything live. The remedy converged, independently, on mechanisms where the granting authority itself observes ownership state (OS-level advisory locks consulting no PID at all) rather than on a validating context inferring liveness from a reusable identifier. The invariant survives generalization past PID specifically: a database session-scoped advisory lock conforms because the database structurally observes connection death; an expiring lease conforms because clock-based reclamation is provable by the grantor; a kernel-held handle conforms because handle death is OS-observable; a fencing token conforms because the token is grantor-issued proof; even a hostname+PID+process-start-time tuple can conform, but only if the start-time genuinely proves the owner's identity to the validating context — provenance of the proof is the invariant, never the identifier's shape.
forbidden: Reclaiming an exclusivity/ownership marker as stale or abandoned based solely on a PID, hostname, or similarly reusable/context-ambiguous identifier, without grantor-observable proof that the prior owner is actually gone
Honoring a marker as currently held, or taking any action on the strength of it, where that determination rests solely on such an identifier rather than on grantor-observable state
Terminating, restarting, or otherwise acting on a process identified only by a marker whose ownership cannot be structurally proven in the current execution context

Treating a specific locking mechanism (e.g. a particular file-lock API) as the invariant itself, such that a structurally-sound but differently-shaped mechanism (a database session lock, a lease, a fencing token) would be read as non-conforming merely for looking different
acceptance: Marker validity is determinable from state the granting authority itself observes (a live connection, an unexpired lease, a held kernel handle, a valid fencing token), not merely from an identifier the validating context alone interprets
A reclamation decision (treating a prior holder as no longer owning the marker) is backed by grantor-observable proof of death or expiry, not by liveness-checking a reusable identifier

Each of the four fleet incidents this standard is evidenced by (indefinite refusal to reclaim a dead owner's lock; termination of a live, unrelated process via a reused identifier; unsound reclaim logic in a one-shot container runtime; a duplicate process spawned because a stale PID file no longer identified anything live) is a non-conforming case under this standard's requirement

A Clank may use any mechanism — OS-level advisory locks, database session-scoped locks, lease services, kernel handles, fencing tokens, or a PID+hostname+start-time tuple where the start-time itself is verified to prove identity — provided the validity/reclamation proof it relies on is structurally observable by the granting authority

evidence.summary: A crash left a lock recording PID 1; every one of ~81 subsequent hourly scheduler fires concluded the prior run was still alive and refused to start, because every Docker container is PID 1 to itself — indefinite starvation, not merely a missed cycle.

A Windows liveness check keyed on a recorded PID could terminate an unrelated process that had since reused that PID — the inverse failure direction from starvation: acting destructively on an unprovable identity.

PID/hostname-based reclaim logic independently proven unsound in Docker's one-shot `run --rm` model, where every container gets a random hostname and PID 1 — a third, independently-discovered instance of the same underlying defect.

A stale PID file no longer identifying any live process let a 15-minute health-check job spawn a duplicate daemon against the same production database — a fourth instance in the same identifier-liveness family.
Fleet-wide convergence on OS-level advisory locks that consult no PID or liveness heuristic at all, structurally observed by the OS rather than inferred by the validating process.

notes: Drafted in a narrowly-commissioned Pass 2.5 task (docs/operations/pass2.5/dossier-ops-d-exclusivity-marker-soundness.md), from the OPS-D candidate card (docs/operations/pass0/candidates/ops-d-exclusivity-marker-soundness.md, ADVANCE), the Pass 1.5 scope-omission resolution (docs/operations/pass1/ops-d-resolution.md), and Pass 2's adversarial review (docs/operations/pass2/review.md, verdict DRAFT AS STD-OPS-COM-004, with explicit drafting constraints this file follows: proposed title kept, exact-distinction rationale sentence kept close to verbatim, minimum acceptance/forbidden concepts all present, no mechanism prescribed beyond the validity-proof requirement). Merges Pass 0A cluster pid-namespace-unsafe-stale-lock-reclaim (docs/operations/pass0/clusters/). Distinct from STD-OPS-COM-001 (execution materialization truth): a Clank deadlocked on a stale, unsound lock can satisfy STD-OPS-COM-001 perfectly (every refused fire is a recorded skip outcome) while starving indefinitely — oem-radar's ~81 refused fires are exactly this; both standards are needed, neither implies the other. COMPLEMENT to clank-architecture Fleet Law 7 (ACTIVE, writer coordination as a principle) and Fleet Law 5 (ACTIVE, single scheduler/notification authority per lane) — neither Law addresses the validity-proof soundness of the coordination primitive itself, and this standard does not restate either. DISTINCT from ADR-0009 (destructive production mutation authority): ADR-0009 governs identity verification before a destructive administrative action; this standard governs ownership-marker validity for routine execution coordination — related in spirit (both forbid acting on an unproven identity), unrelated in scope. Standards Clank defines the semantic invariant; clank-architecture's Fleet Laws and ADRs remain separate authority unless a later governance decision migrates or supersedes them — this standard does not claim to replace clank-architecture, and clank-architecture itself was not modified by this drafting pass. PROPOSED — awaiting the ratification survey and eventual operator ratification; not yet ratified, not self-ratified.
